items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we know that the gradient of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] is

Content:
[MATH: \nabla f(x,y) = (2xy-3x^2) \ \mathbf i + (x^2-2y) \ \mathbf j.]

Content:
How can we reconstruct the function [MATH: f(x,y)] knowing only its gradient?

Content:
Since the components of [MATH: \nabla f] must be the first-order partial derivatives of [MATH: f] with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] respectively, we know that

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} = 2xy-3x^2, \qquad \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}=x^2-2y.}]

Content:
Integrating [MATH: \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x}] with respect to [MATH: x,] treating [MATH: y] as a constant, we get

Content:
[MATH: f(x,y) = \int \left(2xy-3x^2\right) \textrm d x = x^2y -x^3 +g(y),]

Content:
where [MATH: g(y)] is an arbitrary function of [MATH: y.] Intuitively, [MATH: g(y)] contains all the terms that would vanish when differentiated with respect to [MATH: x.]

Content:
Now, differentiating the above with respect to [MATH: y] gives

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} = x^2 + g'(y).]

Content:
So, equating the two expressions for [MATH: \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}] yields
[MATH: \eqalign{
x^2 + g'(y) &= x^2-2y\
g'(y) & = -2y.
}]
Therefore, [MATH: \displaystyle g(y)=\int(-2y) \ \textrm d y = -y^2 +C.]

Content:
This means that
[MATH: f(x,y)=x^2y -x^3-y^2 +C .]

Content:
Note that the above procedure is symmetric with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.] We could have started by integrating [MATH: \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}] with respect to [MATH: y] and then differentiating with respect to [MATH: x.] The final result would have been the same.

sections.readable_text: Find [MATH: f(x,y)] such that [MATH: \nabla f = \mathbf{F},] where [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = 2xy\ \mathbf i + (x^2 - 3)\ \mathbf j .]

sections.normalized_html:
The gradient of the function [MATH: f(x,y)] is defined as

[MATH: \nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}\,\textbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}}\,\textbf{j}.]

Since [MATH: \nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf F(x,y),] the function [MATH: f(x,y)] must satisfy the following system:

[MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = 2xy, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2-3.]

First, we integrate [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}] with respect to [MATH: x.] Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f(x, y)|= ∫(∂f)/(∂x)dx; = ∫2xydx; = x^{2}y + g(y)]

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to [MATH: y,] we obtain

[MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2 + g'(y).]

Taking [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2 -3] into account, we obtain

[MATH: x^{2} + g^{′}(y)|= x^{2} − 3; g^{′}(y)|= − 3; g(y)|= − 3y + C,]

where [MATH: C] is a constant.

Finally, substituting [MATH: g(y)=-3y +C] into our expression for [MATH: f(x,y),] we get [MATH: f(x,y) = x^2y -3y + C.]

Since [MATH: \nabla f(x,y,z) = \mathbf{F}(x,y,z),] the function [MATH: f(x,y,z)] must satisfy the following system: [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = yz, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy+8yz.]

First, we integrate [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}] with respect to [MATH: x.] Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of [MATH: y] and [MATH: z \mathbin{:}] [MATH: f(x, y, z)|= ∫(∂f)/(∂x)dx; = ∫yzdx; = xyz + g(y, z)]

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to [MATH: y,] we obtain [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + \dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}.]

Taking [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2] into account, we obtain

[MATH: xz + (∂g)/(∂y)|= xz + 4z^{2}; (∂g)/(∂y)|= 4z^{2}.]

Now, we integrate [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}] with respect to [MATH: y.] Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of [MATH: z \mathbin{:}] [MATH: g(y, z)|= ∫(∂g)/(∂y)dy; = ∫4z^{2}dy; = 4yz^{2} + h(z)]

Substituting [MATH: g(y,z) = 4yz^2 + h(z)] in the expression for [MATH: f(x, y,z),] we get [MATH: f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + h(z).]

To determine the function [MATH: h(z),] we differentiate [MATH: f(x,y,z)] with respect to [MATH: z.] This gives [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy + 8yz + h'(z).]

Consequently, [MATH: f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + C.]

b. [MATH: f(x, y, z) = x^{2}y − 3yz + Cz]
c. [MATH: f(x, y, z) = x^{2}yz + yz^{2} + C]
d. [MATH: f(x, y, z) = x^{2}y + 2yz + C]
e. [MATH: f(x, y, z) = xy^{2} + 2yz + C]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we know that the gradient of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] is

Content:
[MATH: \nabla f(x,y) = (2xy-3x^2) \ \mathbf i + (x^2-2y) \ \mathbf j.]

Content:
How can we reconstruct the function [MATH: f(x,y)] knowing only its gradient?

Content:
Since the components of [MATH: \nabla f] must be the first-order partial derivatives of [MATH: f] with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] respectively, we know that

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x} = 2xy-3x^2, \qquad \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}=x^2-2y.}]

Content:
Integrating [MATH: \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x}] with respect to [MATH: x,] treating [MATH: y] as a constant, we get

Content:
[MATH: f(x,y) = \int \left(2xy-3x^2\right) \textrm d x = x^2y -x^3 +g(y),]

Content:
where [MATH: g(y)] is an arbitrary function of [MATH: y.] Intuitively, [MATH: g(y)] contains all the terms that would vanish when differentiated with respect to [MATH: x.]

Content:
Now, differentiating the above with respect to [MATH: y] gives

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y} = x^2 + g'(y).]

Content:
So, equating the two expressions for [MATH: \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}] yields
[MATH: \eqalign{
x^2 + g'(y) &= x^2-2y\
g'(y) & = -2y.
}]
Therefore, [MATH: \displaystyle g(y)=\int(-2y) \ \textrm d y = -y^2 +C.]

Content:
This means that
[MATH: f(x,y)=x^2y -x^3-y^2 +C .]

Content:
Note that the above procedure is symmetric with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.] We could have started by integrating [MATH: \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial y}] with respect to [MATH: y] and then differentiating with respect to [MATH: x.] The final result would have been the same.

---

Item 2 — Example: Reconstructing a Two-Variable Function From Its Gradient

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: f(x,y)] such that [MATH: \nabla f = \mathbf{F},] where [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = 2xy\ \mathbf i + (x^2 - 3)\ \mathbf j .]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The gradient of the function [MATH: f(x,y)] is defined as

[MATH: \nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}\,\textbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}}\,\textbf{j}.]

Since [MATH: \nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf F(x,y),] the function [MATH: f(x,y)] must satisfy the following system:

[MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = 2xy, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2-3.]

First, we integrate [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}] with respect to [MATH: x.] Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: f(x, y)|= ∫(∂f)/(∂x)dx; = ∫2xydx; = x^{2}y + g(y)]

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to [MATH: y,] we obtain

[MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2 + g'(y).]

Taking [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = x^2 -3] into account, we obtain

[MATH: x^{2} + g^{′}(y)|= x^{2} − 3; g^{′}(y)|= − 3; g(y)|= − 3y + C,]

where [MATH: C] is a constant.

Finally, substituting [MATH: g(y)=-3y +C] into our expression for [MATH: f(x,y),] we get
[MATH: f(x,y) = x^2y -3y + C.]

Item 5 — Example: Reconstructing a Three-Variable Function From Its Gradient

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: f(x,y,z)] such that [MATH: \nabla f(x,y,z) = \mathbf{F}(x,y,z),] where [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = yz\,\mathbf{i} + (xz + 4z^2)\,\mathbf{j} + (xy+8yz)\,\mathbf{k}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The gradient of the function [MATH: f(x,y,z)] is defined as
[MATH: \nabla f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} \, \mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} \, \mathbf{k}.]

Since [MATH: \nabla f(x,y,z) = \mathbf{F}(x,y,z),] the function [MATH: f(x,y,z)] must satisfy the following system:
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = yz, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy+8yz.]

First, we integrate [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}] with respect to [MATH: x.] Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of [MATH: y] and [MATH: z \mathbin{:}]
[MATH: f(x, y, z)|= ∫(∂f)/(∂x)dx; = ∫yzdx; = xyz + g(y, z)]

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to [MATH: y,] we obtain
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + \dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}.]

Taking [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2] into account, we obtain

[MATH: xz + (∂g)/(∂y)|= xz + 4z^{2}; (∂g)/(∂y)|= 4z^{2}.]

Now, we integrate [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}] with respect to [MATH: y.] Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of [MATH: z \mathbin{:}]
[MATH: g(y, z)|= ∫(∂g)/(∂y)dy; = ∫4z^{2}dy; = 4yz^{2} + h(z)]

Substituting [MATH: g(y,z) = 4yz^2 + h(z)] in the expression for [MATH: f(x, y,z),] we get
[MATH: f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + h(z).]

To determine the function [MATH: h(z),] we differentiate [MATH: f(x,y,z)] with respect to [MATH: z.] This gives
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy + 8yz + h'(z).]

Taking [MATH: \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy+8yz] into account, we obtain
[MATH: xy + 8yz|= xy + 8yz + h^{′}(z); h^{′}(z)|= 0; h(z)|= C,]
where [MATH: C] is a constant.

Consequently,
[MATH: f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + C.]
